about.size: Can reach about 8 feet and 300 lb (FWC).
about.diet: Feeds on fishes and large crustaceans. Adults consume mid-water prey such as mullet, pinfish and marine catfish; crabs are important prey in some seasonal inlet fisheries.
about.depth: Primarily coastal and inshore as adults, with offshore migrations to spawn. Juveniles commonly occupy estuaries and can use freshwater habitats. The current sources do not establish one universal preferred depth range.
about.behavior: Large, slow-growing coastal migratory fish. Adults concentrate in South Florida during cooler months and are widespread along Florida's coast in summer. Juveniles use estuarine and freshwater nursery habitats; adults migrate offshore to spawn. Tarpon gulp air at the surface and tolerate a wide salinity range.
about.spawning: FWC reports a Florida spawning season of May through September. Florida Museum describes typical spawning in May, June and July and extensive migrations to offshore spawning areas. The Keys spring adult run is a seasonal movement pattern and should not be conflated with the full statewide spawning window.
about.regulations_note: Florida tarpon are catch-and-release only except for a single fish harvested in pursuit of a Florida state or world record with a valid tarpon tag. Tarpon over 40 inches must remain in the water unless the tag exception applies.
about.timing_note: Angler lore: patterns reported by local captains and fishing writers, not tested by studies. Numbers are judgment calls to be calibrated against trip logs.

factor_diagnostics.value_notes: Keys tagging (FWC and FIU): most adults arrived in April once water reached 26 C and left in June at 27-29 C, with peak presence in May (26-28 C). Satellite tagging follows a 26 C isotherm. Guides cite 75-80 F (24-27 C), biting best in the low 80s F. Juvenile tarpon left creeks below 20 C, and adults retreat to warmer, deeper water in cold snaps, so cooler water is a hard stop.

factor_diagnostics.value_notes: Keys tagging (FWC and FIU): most adults arrived in April once water reached 26 C and left in June at 27-29 C, with peak presence in May (26-28 C). Satellite tagging follows a 26 C isotherm. Guides cite 75-80 F (24-27 C), biting best in the low 80s F. Juvenile tarpon left creeks below 20 C, and adults retreat to warmer, deeper water in cold snaps, so cooler water is a hard stop.
